name: Evans Gambit
subtitle: Give the bishop a costly invitation.

ideas.idea: The wing pawn invites Black's bishop away from its useful diagonal. Chasing that bishop can help you build a central pawn duo while opening lines for your own pieces. The point is not to attack the bishop forever: spend the gained time on development and central activity.
ideas.structure: A c-pawn advance supports the central break but temporarily takes away a natural knight square. If the centre opens, development matters more than a tidy pawn count. If it stays closed, the missing wing pawn can become a lasting weakness without giving your pieces useful lines.
ideas.pieces: The bishop on c4 points toward the enemy king-side, and a queen can sometimes join pressure on f7 from the b3 diagonal. Castle to connect king safety with rook activity. The queen-side knight needs a route that respects your own central pawns.
ideas.motifs: Central pawn breaks can uncover attacks on the bishop or king. Pressure on f7 can make a developing move come with a threat, but an early queen raid may itself lose time. Count defenders and escape squares before treating a familiar attacking picture as a forced win.
ideas.declined: When Black retreats the bishop without taking, your wing pawn has gained space rather than sacrificed material. Build a healthy centre and complete development. Do not force a second pawn advance simply because you came to practice an attack.
ideas.caution: Black may return the pawn to finish development. Accept that the position has changed: a good centre and active pieces are useful outcomes even when there is no immediate mating attack.

modelGames.summary: A modern revival of the Evans. White uses the tempo gained against the bishop to seize space with e5, keeps Black's king in the centre and opens files just as the defender runs out of time.

moments.title: Space with tempo
moments.note: e5 drives the knight away from f6. White has spent the b-pawn, but in return every move gains time and Black still has not castled.

moments.title: Pressure on g7
moments.note: The queen targets g7, provoking a weakening pawn move. Small concessions around the king add up when the attacker is ahead in development.

moments.title: No castling allowed
moments.note: The bishop takes the f8 square away from Black's king. White is even willing to let the e5 pawn go if it keeps the king stuck in the centre.

moments.title: Files open, king exposed
moments.note: Pawn exchanges in the centre have opened lines, and the queen moves to the e-file. The king in the middle is now the main target.

moments.title: Everything points at e6
moments.note: Queen, rook and knight all aim at the bishop on e6, and Bc4 would pin it to the king. Black has a pawn more, but no way to untangle in time.

modelGames.summary: Black meets the gambit with a timely ...d5, gives the pawn back and castles. With his king safe, he targets White's isolated central pawns and ends up attacking White's king.

moments.title: Return the pawn, free the game
moments.note: ...d5 hands a pawn back but opens lines for Black's pieces. Defenders rarely hold every gambit pawn; they aim for safe development instead.

moments.title: King safety first
moments.note: Black castles before anything else. Once the king is tucked away, White's lead in development has no obvious target.

moments.title: Targets in White's centre
moments.note: White's d-pawns look imposing but cannot be supported by other pawns. Black's rook on the e-file and knight heading for f5 are ready to work against them.

moments.title: A queen next to the king
moments.note: The black queen settles on h3, right next to White's king. Defending a gambit often ends with the defender taking over the initiative.

moments.title: Mate on g2 is coming
moments.note: The knight joins the queen, threatening mate on g2. Black's pieces are coordinated while White's are scattered—the opposite of what the gambit intended.
